title: tiktoken — fast BPE tokeniser for OpenAI models (encodings o200k_base, cl100k_base)
key_findings: Version 0.14.0 installed from PyPI and run locally; MIT licence confirmed from the repository LICENSE file.
Its model map assigns o200k_base to gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.5, o-series and gpt-5 prefixes and cl100k_base to gpt-4/gpt-3.5; gpt-oss uses an o200k_harmony variant.
ATHAR measurement: Arabic/English token ratio 1.18 with o200k_base vs 2.33 with cl100k_base on the 18-pair core set (see ARABIC_TOKEN_COST_MEASUREMENT.md).
athar_applications: Use o200k_base (not cl100k_base) when estimating OpenAI-family Arabic costs; the 2023 '~3x' figure describes the older encoding only.
limitations: The library's model map ends at the gpt-5 prefix; tokenisers of newer OpenAI API models listed on the pricing page (gpt-6.x) are not published, so their Arabic behaviour is unknown.

title: Hugging Face tokenizers library (Rust/Python)
key_findings: Version 0.23.3 installed from PyPI; loads a model's tokenizer.json (pure data) without executing model code — allowing token counts without transformers or trust_remote_code.
Used with add_special_tokens=False to count raw text tokens for 10 open-model tokenisers in the ATHAR measurement.
athar_applications: Safe, reproducible way to re-run Arabic token measurements whenever a candidate open model changes.
limitations: Counts exclude chat-template tokens added by each model's prompt format; per-message overhead must be added separately.

title: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B — Hugging Face model cards and tokenizer files
key_findings: Both repositories are non-gated and Apache-2.0 per the Hub API; tokenizer.json downloaded at a pinned commit.
Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 share an identical 151,643-entry BPE vocabulary in our measurement (identical counts on all 34 items).
ATHAR measurement: Arabic/English ratio 1.31 overall; 1.43–1.49 for Gulf/Egyptian/Levantine dialogue; 1.72 for UI strings.
athar_applications: Mid-range Arabic efficiency; candidate for self-hosted intent classification if hosting in-region is needed.
limitations: Tokenizer efficiency says nothing about Arabic output quality or safety; evaluate separately (see library 07 W2 sources).

title: DeepSeek-V3.1 — Hugging Face model repository and tokenizer
key_findings: Non-gated, MIT per Hub API card data; 128,000-entry BPE vocabulary (+818 added tokens).
ATHAR measurement: Arabic/English ratio 1.34 overall, 1.83 for UI strings.
athar_applications: Reference point only; data-residency and child-safety questions (library 11) dominate any use decision.
limitations: The repository also contains custom modelling code; ATHAR fetched only tokenizer.json and executed nothing.

title: Mistral-Nemo-Instruct-2407 — model card (Tekken tokenizer, 2^17 vocabulary)
key_findings: Model card states a vocabulary of about 2^17 (~128k); repository non-gated, Apache-2.0.
ATHAR measurement: lowest premium among non-Arabic-specialised tokenisers — Arabic/English ratio 1.09 overall, 1.11–1.22 for dialect dialogue.
athar_applications: Shows that a general multilingual tokenizer can reach near-parity for Arabic; useful benchmark when negotiating with vendors.
limitations: Mistral's hosted API models may use different tokenisers; this measures the open 2407 release only.

title: phi-4 — model card
key_findings: MIT licence; released 12 Dec 2024; card says multilingual data is about 8% of training data and the model is not intended for multilingual use.
ATHAR measurement: its tokenizer gave counts identical to cl100k_base on all 34 items (ratio 2.33), i.e. a 100k-class vocabulary with the old Arabic premium.
athar_applications: Negative example: small English-centric models carry the ~2.3–2.6x Arabic premium and should not be chosen for Arabic dialogue.
limitations: The card does not name the tokenizer; equivalence with cl100k_base is our empirical observation on this test set.

title: gpt-oss-20b — Hugging Face model repository and tokenizer
key_findings: Non-gated, Apache-2.0; tokenizer.json with a 199,998-entry vocabulary.
ATHAR measurement: counts identical to tiktoken o200k_base on all items (ratio 1.18), confirming the o200k family's Arabic behaviour on an open-weight model.
athar_applications: Self-hostable open-weight option whose Arabic token cost matches OpenAI's current-generation published encoding.
limitations: Arabic quality and child-safety behaviour not evaluated here.

title: Jais family (jais-family-13b-chat) — model card incl. Arabic tokenizer expansion note
key_findings: Repository moved from inceptionai/ to inception42/ (HTTP 307 redirect observed); jais-family-13b-chat is non-gated, Apache-2.0, 84,992-token vocabulary.
Card states that the jais-adapted models add 32,000 Arabic tokens to the Llama-2 tokenizer, reporting >3x better fertility/compute efficiency.
ATHAR measurement: Arabic needs FEWER tokens than the parallel English (ratio 0.88 overall; 0.77 informal dialect argument).
athar_applications: Arabic-centric tokenisers remove the language premium entirely; relevant for any self-hosted Arabic classifier or dialogue model.
limitations: Some Jais repositories (jais-13b-chat, Jais-2-8B-Chat, jais-adapted-*) are gated ('auto') and were not downloaded; repository also contains custom code (not executed). The fully diacritised text inflated its count 5.9x vs English — worst of all tokenisers.

title: Fanar-1-9B-Instruct — model card (continual pre-training of gemma-2-9b; Apache-2.0)
key_findings: Card: continually pre-trained from google/gemma-2-9b on ~1T tokens (≈515B English, 410B Arabic, 102B code), with attention to MSA and Gulf, Levantine and Egyptian dialects; Apache-2.0.
Non-gated tokenizer (128,256 entries) — gives an openly downloadable proxy for the gated Gemma-2 tokenizer family.
ATHAR measurement: Arabic/English ratio 1.24 overall; 1.25–1.32 across dialects.
athar_applications: Candidate regional model (Qatar) for intent classification or dialogue if data-residency in the Gulf is required (to be weighed with library 11).
limitations: That Fanar-1 reuses the Gemma-2 tokenizer unchanged is our inference from the base-model statement and vocabulary size; not stated explicitly in the card.

AUDIT-W2 2026-10-27: MAJOR - the 'Gemma-2 tokenizer proxy' claim is contradicted by the published configs: Fanar-1-9B(-Instruct) config.json vocab_size = 128,256, whereas gemma-2-9b (unsloth mirror) config.json vocab_size = 256,000. The Fanar-1 tokenizer is therefore NOT the Gemma-2 tokenizer (tokenizer_class is GemmaTokenizer, but the vocabulary differs). The 1.24 ratio measured with it says nothing about Gemma-2. (Fanar-2-27B and Gemma-3 both report 262,208, so the Fanar-2->Gemma-3 proxy remains plausible.) Model-card facts (gemma-2-9b base, ~1T tokens = 515B EN / 410B AR / 102B code, Apache-2.0, not gated) verified. Fix needed in 10/ARABIC_TOKEN_COST_MEASUREMENT.md line 49 (annotated by audit).

title: ALLaM-7B-Instruct-preview — tokenizer.model (SentencePiece, 64k)
key_findings: Non-gated, Apache-2.0 per Hub API; the repository ships only a SentencePiece tokenizer.model (64,000 pieces), read with the sentencepiece library.
ATHAR measurement: ratio 0.88 overall and the most robust tokenizer for fully diacritised text (2.3x vs 3.0–5.9x for others).
athar_applications: Best option tested if ATHAR ever ships fully vocalised MSA (e.g., for 13–15 readers) through a model.
limitations: Card states 5.2T training tokens; quality/safety not assessed here. Licence file details remain a G15 item handled by W2-LEGAL.

title: Jais-3-32B and Fanar-2-27B-Instruct — tokenizer files (2025–2026 releases)
key_findings: Both non-gated, Apache-2.0. Jais-3-32B: 250,000-entry BPE with NFC normaliser; ratio 0.89 overall.
Fanar-2-27B card: continually pre-trained from gemma-3-27b-pt on ~166B Arabic/English/code tokens; 262,144-entry vocabulary; ratio 1.21 overall (proxy for the gated Gemma-3 tokenizer).
athar_applications: Confirms the split: Arabic-built vocabularies reach parity (<1.0); Arabic continual pre-training on a Gemma base keeps a ~1.2x premium.
limitations: Model-card benchmark tables are vendor-reported; not used here.

title: Claude Platform Docs — Pricing (model prices, batch, caching, tokenizer note)
key_findings: Prices read 2026-10-27 (USD/MTok, input/output): Haiku 5.5 $0.10/$0.50 (≤100K prompt), Sonnet 5.5 $2/$10, Opus 5.5 $4/$20; batch = 50% of base; cache reads $0.01/$0.10/$0.20 respectively.
States that Opus 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer producing about 30% more tokens for the same text, so per-token prices are not comparable across generations.
US-only inference adds a 1.1x multiplier on 4.6+ models.
athar_applications: Inputs to the cost table in ARABIC_TOKEN_COST_MEASUREMENT.md; Anthropic's tokenizer is not public, so Arabic counts must be measured with the free count_tokens endpoint (not done in this session: no API key).
limitations: Prices change; page shows no 'last updated' date. Disclosure: Anthropic makes the model that drafted this record — reported neutrally.

title: Claude Platform Docs — Token counting (messages.count_tokens)
key_findings: The endpoint is free, takes the same inputs as message creation and returns an estimated input-token count; rate-limited separately (5,000–20,000 RPM by tier).
No offline tokenizer is documented; counts must be obtained per model ID via the API.
athar_applications: Concrete next step for G28: run token_test_set.jsonl through count_tokens for each candidate Claude model (needs an API key).
limitations: Counts are estimates and may include system-added tokens that are not billed.

title: OpenAI API — Pricing page
key_findings: Standard-tier text prices read 2026-10-27 (USD per 1M tokens, input/cached/output): gpt-6-luna $0.10/$0.01/$0.50; gpt-6.1-terra $1.00/$0.05/$5.00; gpt-6.1-sol $2.00/$0.10/$10.00; gpt-6-astra $10/$1/$50.
No GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini or GPT-5 mini/nano text prices are listed on the current page.
athar_applications: Inputs to the ATHAR cost table; combine with measured token ratios only for models whose tokenizer is known.
limitations: The tokeniser of the gpt-6.x models is not published (tiktoken maps only up to the gpt-5 prefix); Arabic ratios for them are unmeasured.

title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
key_findings: Analyses cost and utility of a commercial LLM API across 22 typologically diverse languages; token counts for equivalent content vary widely by language.
Concludes that speakers of many supported languages are charged more while getting poorer results, often in regions where the API is least affordable.
athar_applications: Frames G28 as an equity issue as well as a cost one: Arabic teen users should not receive shorter or worse AI turns because of tokenisation.
limitations: Measured 2023-era OpenAI tokenisers; our 2026 measurement shows the o200k generation has much reduced the Arabic premium.

title: AraToken: Optimizing Arabic Tokenization with Normalization Pipeline and Language Extension for Qwen3
key_findings: Preprint (20 Dec 2025): an Arabic SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer with normalisation of alif variants, diacritics and Arabic-Indic digits reports 1.199 tokens/word vs 1.35 unnormalised.
Extends Qwen3-0.6B's vocabulary with Arabic tokens; reports evaluation-loss reduction within 800 steps.
athar_applications: Supports ATHAR's own finding that diacritics and digit variants are the main drivers of token inflation; normalise player text before classification.
limitations: Not peer-reviewed; the abstract's '18% lower fertility' does not match its own reported numbers (≈11%).

title: inkjs 2.4.0 (npm) — full build with in-JavaScript ink compiler
key_findings: Installed 2.4.0 (registry modified 2026-02-17) with --ignore-scripts; the 'inkjs/full' Compiler compiled and ran an Arabic story: Arabic VAR/LIST/knot/function names, Arabic choices, tags and Eastern-Arabic digits in text all worked; state JSON keeps Arabic keys.

Its identifier grammar defines the Arabic range as U+0600–U+06FF only: identifiers using Arabic Supplement letters (U+0750+), presentation forms (U+FExx, typical of PDF copy-paste), RLM/ZWNJ inside names fail to compile.
Diacritics are part of identifiers: a variable declared with shadda/kasra is a different name from the undiacritised spelling (compile error 'Unresolved variable').
athar_applications: Confirms ink+inkjs for authored Arabic scenes; add a pre-compile normaliser (strip bidi marks/ZWNJ in identifiers, NFKC-fold presentation forms, forbid harakat in identifiers) and keep identifiers ASCII where content is machine-generated.
limitations: Gotcha found: a condition placed after the choice bracket ('* [text] {cond}') is printed as literal 'true' in output rather than gating the choice; authors must write '* {cond} [text]'. Language-independent but easy for RTL writers to misplace.

title: Inky 0.15.2 source (inkle/inky) — editor component and i18n files
key_findings: Shallow clone at commit 3d46aa9 (2026-05-05): package version 0.15.2, MIT per README; UI translations exist only for fi-FI, ru-RU and zh-CN (no Arabic UI).

The editor embeds Ace v1.2.6 (per its VERSION file); grep finds no bidi handler, and our Chromium render of that Ace build shows Arabic lines laid out LTR, with mixed Arabic/Latin runs in confusing order and no RTL option.

Ace added bidirectional text support in v1.2.9 (2017) and an 'rtl' option in v1.4.3 (2019) per Ace's CHANGELOG; current ace-builds 1.43.4 renders the same ink lines right-aligned with correct bidi when rtlText/rtl are set.
athar_applications: Arabic writers should not author in stock Inky; an ATHAR ink field should use a modern editor component (Ace ≥1.4.3 with rtl, or CodeMirror 6) with bidi enabled.
limitations: Rendering tested in headless Chromium only, not in the packaged Electron app; Inky's Electron/Chromium may still apply some bidi to plain text.

title: Ace editor CHANGELOG (bidirectional text 1.2.9; rtl option 1.4.3) and ace-builds 1.43.4
key_findings: CHANGELOG records 'added support for bidirectional text' in 1.2.9 (2017-10-17) and 'add rtl option' in 1.4.3 (2019-02-21); later entries fix the bidi handler and render bidi control characters visibly.
ace-builds 1.43.4 (BSD-3-Clause) with ext-rtl: rtlText+rtl produced right-aligned Arabic ink source with correctly ordered mixed runs in our test.
athar_applications: If ATHAR's authoring tool embeds a code-style editor for ink/JSON snippets, use a modern Ace with RTL options or equivalent.
limitations: Monospace Arabic rendering in code editors remains less legible than proportional text; form-based authoring stays preferable for writers.

title: YarnSpinner.Console (ysc) 3.2.2 — command-line compiler/runner for Yarn Spinner
key_findings: 3.2.2 (published 2026-05-05, MIT, targets net9.0) run with the official .NET 9.0.22 runtime: Arabic node titles, $Arabic variables, Arabic options and '#تناقض' hashtags compiled and ran; string table (CSV and XLSX) preserved Arabic text with line IDs.

Failures: Eastern-Arabic digits are not number literals (syntax error); RLM inside a variable name is a token error; a node title in presentation forms or containing ZWNJ silently becomes a different node (start-node lookup fails).
An undeclared variable spelled without the diacritics of a declared one only raises a compile WARNING and runs, silently reading the wrong variable — a real hazard for Arabic writers.
athar_applications: Yarn's per-line ID + string-table model is the right localisation pattern; but if used, ATHAR must treat 'used but not declared' warnings as errors and normalise identifiers.
limitations: The console runner prints '{0}' placeholders instead of substituting values and does not process [plural]/[select] markup — substitution belongs to the game runtime (Unity/Godot), so web use requires a JS runtime that was not tested.

title: Twine 2.12.1 source — bundled story formats list and publish template substitution
key_findings: Commit 2c3b801 (2026-10-06), version 2.12.1: bundled formats are Chapbook 1.2.3/2.3.1, Harlowe 1.2.4/2.1.0/3.3.9, Paperthin 1.0.0, Snowman 1.5.0/2.1.4, SugarCube 1.0.35/2.37.3.
Editor source (src/) contains no rtl/dir/bidi handling; the CodeMirror 5 options set no direction; publishing only substitutes {{STORY_NAME}} and {{STORY_DATA}} into the format template.
athar_applications: Twine can be used only for throwaway branching sketches by Arabic writers; RTL must be added per story via stylesheet.
limitations: Editor not run interactively; conclusions from source inspection plus rendering of published HTML.

title: Twine story formats Harlowe 3.3.9, SugarCube 2.37.3, Chapbook 2.3.1, Snowman 2.1.4 — format.js sources (RTL inspection and render test)
license: Harlowe: Zlib; SugarCube: BSD-2-Clause; Snowman: MIT; Chapbook: not stated in format.js
key_findings: None of the four templates sets dir or lang on <html>; with Arabic text all render LTR (computed direction ltr) until a story stylesheet sets direction:rtl; SugarCube's only 'RTL' token is its '<-' link-arrow lexer, not text direction.

Arabic variable names fail in Harlowe ($عدد_الأدلة printed literally plus a syntax error; identifier class covers \w and Latin-1/Hungarian letters) and in SugarCube (identifier regex is [$A-Z_a-z][$0-9A-Z_a-z]*: '<<set>> bad evaluation'); they work in Chapbook and Snowman.
Arabic passage names and Arabic link text work in all four formats after the click test.
athar_applications: If Twine is used for prototypes: choose Chapbook or Snowman, keep variable names ASCII, and add 'html{direction:rtl}' plus <bdi> around Latin IDs in the story stylesheet.
limitations: Licences of Harlowe/SugarCube/Snowman read from format.js metadata; Chapbook's format.js has no license field (see ATH-SRC-1837).

title: Unicode Standard Annex #9: Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (Revision 52, Unicode 18.0.0)
key_findings: Revision 52 dated 2026-09-01 (Unicode 18.0.0) defines how mixed RTL/LTR text is ordered for display while stored in logical order.
Defines isolates (LRI, RLI, FSI … PDI), which stop inserted text from reordering its surroundings, as distinct from older embeddings/overrides and the invisible marks LRM/RLM/ALM.
athar_applications: Normative basis for ATHAR's rule: insert every variable or Latin ID into Arabic templates inside an isolate (<bdi> or FSI…PDI), never with bare RLM.
limitations: Unicode terms of use apply to reproduction of the text.

title: Inline markup and bidirectional text in HTML (W3C Internationalization article)
key_findings: For text of known direction, wrap opposite-direction phrases in an element with dir; for runtime data of unknown direction use dir=auto on the containing element or wrap it in <bdi> (which behaves as dir=auto).
Use Unicode isolate controls only where markup is impossible (e.g., title, attribute values); avoid RLE/LRE; RLM/LRM do not fix nesting.
athar_applications: Directly specifies the rendering rule for evidence IDs, Latin names and numbers in ATHAR evidence cards and choices.
limitations: Date and author not shown on fetched page; W3C document licence applies.

title: Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements (W3C Group Draft Note, 2 Oct 2025)
key_findings: Documents three digit families (European, Arabic-Indic, Extended Arabic-Indic) whose different bidi categories change how mixed text orders, plus region-specific separators and symbol placement.
Covers line breaking in mixed text, justification (kashida/tatweel), joining controls (ZWNJ/ZWJ), and advises avoiding deprecated presentation forms and U+FEFF.
athar_applications: Reference for ATHAR's digit-choice setting, % placement and why presentation forms must be normalised before ink/Yarn compilation.
limitations: Group Draft Note — not a W3C Recommendation; may change.

title: Hint Systems May Negatively Impact Performance in Educational Games — full text (author-hosted copy)
publisher: ACM (L@S 2014); copy hosted by UW Center for Game Science
key_findings: Full text read (closes part of G21): 2x2 design (embedded 'message in a bottle' vs earned robot hints x concrete 'bottom-out' vs abstract question-style 'pointing' hints) plus a no-hint baseline; 10,000 players per condition sampled from 79,895 on BrainPOP.

All four hint conditions had slightly lower win rates than no hints (e.g., intro levels 89.45% baseline vs ~87.8–88.5%; effect sizes very small, V≤0.04); earned hints increased play time slightly (median 192 vs 178 s) and were hoarded and used mostly when struggling (~75–80%).

Concrete hints were used more and led to faster wins than abstract hints; hints were single, non-adaptive, one per level and not tied to the player's partial solution — the authors name this as a likely cause.

Cites earlier findings in the same game that adding a help button reduced levels completed by 12% and play time by 15% although only 31% clicked it, and a studio that reduced hint avoidance by renaming 'hint' to 'advice'.
athar_applications: The negative result concerns static, non-adaptive hints for children ~3-minute sessions; it does not refute ATHAR's dependency-chart, node-specific ladder but keeps the 'no explicit hints' arm in H1 mandatory.
Avoid the word 'تلميح' as a punitive button label; frame help diegetically (ally advice) — supported by the renaming anecdote.
limitations: Short sessions (~3 min average), elementary-age players, math puzzle game, no pre/post test; level completion used as proxy for learning.

title: Optimizing Challenge in an Educational Game Using Large-Scale Design Experiments — full text (course-hosted copy)
key_findings: Full text read (closes part of G21): two online experiments (~10K and ~70K players) of a number-line math game found engagement rose almost linearly as the game got easier; the inverted-U quadratic fit was not significant (p=0.8).
The most engaging (easiest) conditions produced the slowest learning curves; very short time limits were the most disengaging factor; more item variety (less repetition) increased engagement.

Authors propose four hypotheses: optimal success may be >90%; success attributable to the player's own competence motivates more; challenge-seeking may need expertise (make first levels very easy); and 'feedforward' — telling players the challenge level in advance — may let them value harder tasks.
athar_applications: Supports H5 (declared difficulty / 'challenge' option) and an easy first case; warns against tuning ATHAR cases on play-time alone.
limitations: Anonymous web players, mostly short sessions; learning measured as within-game improvement; self-selection by restarting into new conditions noted by authors.

title: Effective player guidance in logic puzzles (PhD thesis)
key_findings: An in-person Sudoku study found players were unsystematic, idiosyncratic and error-prone — unlike the assumptions in solver-based player models.

A new hint approach that steers players toward an easier available deduction (instead of filling the next cell) was as helpful as the existing system, improved player experience, felt less like cheating, and was chosen significantly more often (four studies, two puzzle types).
athar_applications: Direct support for ATHAR hint levels 1–3: point to an available deduction (which evidence/relation), do not reveal the answer node.
limitations: Pen-and-paper logic puzzles, not narrative deduction; sample details not in the abstract (abstract-level reading only). Supervisors: Gent, Jefferson, May, Hinrichs; awarded 12 June 2024.

title: Understanding how players solve puzzles (ExCoS 2025 workshop abstract)
publisher: University of St Andrews research portal (Workshop on Explanations with Constraints and Satisfiability)
key_findings: Two-page abstract on Binairo players using hints in unfamiliar puzzles: hint users performed better, completed more puzzles and appeared more strategic.
athar_applications: Weak supporting signal that well-designed deduction hints need not reduce performance (contrast with ATH-SRC-1925).
limitations: Abstract only; correlational; no sample size reported on the page.

title: An Adaptive Hint System for Puzzle Games: A Multimodal-based Approach
key_findings: Survey of 104 players: 66.3% said hints did not fit their needs in timing, presentation or access; players preferred concise, accurate, implicit, text-based hints that do not reveal the whole puzzle.
Industry review of hint triggers (on request, paid, delayed, on failure, on loading) with drawbacks of each; e.g., 'on failure' exposes repeated failure.
A camera-based stuck detector (78% test accuracy) with researcher-triggered hints gave better experience ratings in a 30-person study (5 per game per group).
athar_applications: Supports ATHAR's telemetry-triggered offer of level-1 hints but argues for 'offer, don't impose'; camera-based detection is excluded for minors on privacy grounds.
limitations: Very small experimental groups; Likert ratings; researcher-written hints. Venue identified via Crossref, PDF via author's faculty page.

title: Designing effective hints systems (M.S. thesis)
key_findings: In a notoriously difficult puzzle game, abstract hints were rated worse than receiving no hint; concrete hints were rated more helpful.
Player experience depended mainly on the game itself; letting players choose their hint type did not significantly change experience.
athar_applications: Warns that ATHAR's level-1 'where to look' questions must still be specific to the current node; vague prompts can be worse than nothing.
limitations: Master's thesis; single game; abstract-level reading.

title: Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems
publisher: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 26(1), 205–223
key_findings: A 'Help Tutor' giving real-time feedback on students' help-seeking made their use of on-demand help more deliberate, and the effect persisted after feedback stopped — but domain learning did not improve.
The authors conclude on-demand, principle-based help is less central to learning than once assumed, while still useful in some situations.
athar_applications: Do not expect a better hint ladder alone to raise learning; measure help-seeking as a metacognitive behaviour in its own right (e.g., 'hint before trying' rate).
limitations: Tutoring-system (algebra/geometry) context; abstract-level reading.

title: Estrategias de pistas en escape rooms educativas: un enfoque de minería de procesos (Hint strategies in educational escape rooms: a process mining approach)
publisher: Revista de Educación (Ministerio de Educación, España), no. 405
key_findings: Trace data from four online university-level educational escape rooms (Escapp platform): overall hint use was low; students mostly relied on their own problem solving.
Hint requests co-occurred with longer play and more failed attempts (correlational).
athar_applications: Expect low voluntary hint uptake; ATHAR telemetry should model hint requests as signals of struggle, not as causes of slower progress.
limitations: Participant count not on the page; university students; DOI 10.4438/1988-592X-RE-2024-405-626 printed on the page but not resolvable in Crossref during this session.

title: How General Game Expertise Shapes Player Experience and Problem-Solving Across Different Onboarding Approaches in a Puzzle Video Game
key_findings: 120+ players of Baba Is You under three onboarding conditions: self-reported gaming expertise predicted higher enjoyment, more levels completed and more exploratory tinkering; some effects differed by onboarding condition.
athar_applications: Teen samples will vary widely in gaming expertise; record it as a covariate in every ATHAR hint/difficulty experiment and consider an optional 'experienced player' track.
limitations: Abstract-level reading; licence stated per PDF (not read). Related ThinkyCon 2025 talk by the same group describes interviews with 25 puzzle developers.

title: Designed to Fail: Puzzle Game Developers' Perspectives on Designing Challenge and Failure
publisher: ACM (FDG 2026, Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games)
key_findings: Bibliographic record and CC BY 4.0 licence confirmed via Crossref; the ThinkyCon 2025 talk page by the same authors describes interviews with 25 puzzle-game developers about how puzzles teach and how players progress.
athar_applications: Candidate primary source on how professional puzzle designers deliberately design failure — to read in full before finalising ATHAR's 'every error yields information' rule.
limitations: Content NOT read: ACM DL and researchr.org blocked automated fetch; no findings are claimed from it.

title: The Burden of Proof: Narrative Deduction Mechanics for Detective Games (GDC 2022 session page)
key_findings: Session description: addresses the 'problem of proof' — how players demonstrate they solved a crime and how the game responds when they have not — using inkle's Overboard!, where players assemble and refine a solution from evidence and speculation.
Describes a deduction system giving specific feedback without removing player creativity, generalisable to conventional detective stories.
athar_applications: Closest professional precedent for ATHAR's 'argument screen' with specific post-verdict feedback; watch the talk before finalising the review screen.
limitations: Only the session description was read; video not watched (GDC Vault requires login; tagged 'free content' but access not confirmed).

title: The Case of the Golden Idol — 'Redux' update announcements (official Steam news, Oct 2024)
key_findings: Official posts (3 and 10 Oct 2024) describe Redux: a UI overhaul for readability at smaller resolutions, a new hint system, markers showing which objects are interactable ('no more guessing or using guides'), and 13 new localisations; players may still launch the classic version.
Golden Idol content had been brought to mobile via a Netflix partnership before Redux.
athar_applications: Evidence that the leading deduction game added hints, interactable markers and small-screen readability after launch — supports ATHAR shipping an optional hint ladder and visible interactables from v0.1.
limitations: Hint-system mechanics are not described in the posts; Arabic is not among the listed languages.

title: The Roottrees are Dead — developer update notes on the hint system (official Steam news, Jan–Feb 2025) and Adventure Game Hotspot review
key_findings: Developer patch notes (16 Jan–7 Feb 2025) repeatedly fix and tune hints, including 'A hint is now skipped if you've figured out a later step' and a fix for hints not appearing for players who needed them.

Review: an always-available, penalty-free hint system checks the player's evidence and not-yet-locked profiles and escalates from subtle nudges to direct answers; correct profiles are confirmed and locked intermittently, frequently early and less often later.
athar_applications: Hint ladder must be state-aware (skip hints for nodes already solved) — add to ATHAR rule set; 'lock-in' frequency that decreases over the game is a second, published pattern for batch validation (H2).
limitations: Review is journalism (grade D-level for mechanics description); patch notes are terse.

title: The Rise of the Golden Idol Preview – The Adventure Continues (GamingTrend)
key_findings: Reviewer reports filling the last gaps of a deduction by trying keyword combinations and letting the system say right or wrong, and calls this trial-and-error endgame a genre-wide weakness.
athar_applications: Independent confirmation of the brute-force risk that ATHAR's batch validation and 'circular switching' telemetry are meant to catch.
limitations: Preview of a demo; opinion.

title: ThinkyCon 2025 programme and talk pages ('Playful Puzzle Mechanics', 'Under the Hood of Stumbling in Puzzle Games')
key_findings: Programme of 36 recorded talks (5–7 Nov 2025); 'Playful Puzzle Mechanics' (Anderson, Carpenter, Eshgarf) covers an onboarding study in Baba Is You and interviews with 25 puzzle developers; 'Under the Hood of Stumbling' (Jackson Nagy) covers player heuristics and when they mislead.
Talk pages embed YouTube recordings (e.g., I9C1OKjqtMg, yq4Rj4-FGK8).
athar_applications: Viewing list for the ATHAR designer (human task): both talks address where players get stuck.
limitations: Only titles/descriptions read; no findings claimed from the videos.

title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity
key_findings: Target article synthesising many paradigms: when rehearsal and chunking are blocked, a central short-term storage limit averages about four chunks (range roughly three to five), smaller than Miller's 'seven'.
athar_applications: Design ceiling for ATHAR: the argument screen should ask the player to hold/compare at most ~3–4 items at once (claim + 2–3 evidence cards); the evidence board must externalise everything else (pins, notes, timeline).
limitations: Capacity in chunks depends on expertise and grouping; it is not a direct cap on how many evidence items a case file may contain.

title: Does presentation size of instructional materials influence the split-attention effect?
key_findings: 146 university students, large vs small presentation x split vs integrated format: no significant effects of format, size or interaction on retention, comprehension or extraneous load; Bayesian analyses mostly favoured the null.
Authors call for a more nuanced view of the split-attention effect and testing even smaller sizes.
athar_applications: Caution: 'integrate text and graphic' is good practice but its benefit on small sizes is not established; ATHAR should A/B test evidence-card layouts on real phones rather than assume.
limitations: Both sizes shown on a 22-inch monitor (smallest 326×192 mm) — far larger than a phone; adults, not teens.

title: Don't throw away your printed books: A meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension
key_findings: 54 studies (2000–2017; 171,055 participants): reading comprehension was lower on screens than on paper (Hedges' g ≈ −0.21).
The screen disadvantage was larger under time constraints than with self-paced reading, held for informational (not purely narrative) texts, and grew over the period studied.
athar_applications: Evidence documents in ATHAR are informational texts: avoid timers on evidence reading, allow self-paced re-reading, and keep critical documents short.
limitations: Volume 25, pages 23–38 confirmed via Crossref; 'screens' include computers and e-readers, not only phones; mostly pre-2018 studies.

title: Reading Content on Mobile Devices
key_findings: Study of 276 participants reading easy and hard articles: comprehension on phones was practically equal to computers (≈3 points higher on mobile, statistically but not practically significant).
Hard articles were read more slowly on mobile (about 30 ms more per word), suggesting readers slow down to keep comprehension as complexity rises.
athar_applications: Phones are acceptable for case-file reading if text is short and difficult passages allow extra time (no reading timers).
limitations: Industry UX study, English readers, adults, not peer reviewed; contrasts with older studies that found mobile impairment.

title: The Study of Cognitive Load and Learning Achievement in Multimedia Courseware on Different Size Mobile Devices (Master's thesis, NCTU)
key_findings: Quasi-experiment with 97 first-year senior-high students: 3.5-inch and 2.8-inch screens yielded lower cognitive load and better achievement than a 2.0-inch screen; courseware with 4 information elements outperformed 2 elements.
athar_applications: Historical support that very small screens raise load for adolescents; modern phones exceed these sizes, so the practical constraint today is information density per view rather than screen size.
limitations: 2008 devices; Taiwanese students; master's thesis; abstract only.

title: StatCounter Global Stats — Mobile operating system market share by country (Sep 2026: Saudi Arabia, UAE, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Iraq)
key_findings: September 2026 Android vs iOS share of mobile web page views: Saudi Arabia 48.4% vs 51.6%; UAE 73.3% vs 26.7%; Egypt 83.4% vs 16.6%; Jordan 77.4% vs 22.6%; Lebanon 72.9% vs 27.1%; Morocco 74.0% vs 26.0%; Iraq 86.3% vs 13.6%.
Only Saudi Arabia shows an iOS majority among the countries checked.
athar_applications: Default test matrix: low/mid Android Chrome (Egypt/Iraq/Morocco/Jordan) plus iOS Safari (Saudi Arabia). Safari's storage-eviction rules (ATH-SRC-0964, ATH-SRC-1947) matter most for the Saudi market.
limitations: Measures page-view share on sites using StatCounter, all ages — not teens and not device ownership; no reuse licence stated ('All rights reserved').

title: Learn PWA (web.dev course)
key_findings: Course chapters cover service workers, Cache Storage, serving strategies, Workbox, offline data (IndexedDB, Storage Manager, Persistent Storage, Content Indexing), installation, web app manifest, install prompt, updates and detection of installed state.
athar_applications: Checklist for ATHAR's PWA: case packs in Cache Storage, ledger in IndexedDB, persist() request, explicit update flow for case-package versions.
limitations: No authors or dates shown; Chrome-centric — Safari support differs (see ATH-SRC-1947).

title: Updates to Storage Policy (WebKit blog)
key_findings: From Safari 17 / iOS 17: per-origin quota up to 60% of disk for browser apps (15% for other apps), overall up to 80%/20%; Home Screen web apps get the same quotas as in the browser.

Origins are best-effort by default; navigator.storage.persist() is granted by heuristics, one of which is being opened as a Home Screen web app; eviction can follow quota/system pressure or periods without user interaction (ITP).
athar_applications: For Saudi (iOS-majority) users, prompt 'Add to Home Screen' before downloading case packs and request persist(); keep server-side sync of progress.
limitations: Policy may change in later iOS versions; check before launch.

title: Workbox — service worker libraries (Chrome for Developers) and workbox-sw 7.4.1 (npm)
key_findings: Production-ready service worker libraries and tooling from the Chrome team for routing and caching; npm workbox-sw 7.4.1 lists MIT.
athar_applications: Default implementation path for ATHAR's cache-first case packs and background telemetry sync.
limitations: Licence taken from npm metadata, not the docs page.

title: SIL Open Font License 1.1 — OFL-FAQ 1.1-update7 (openfontlicense.org)
key_findings: OFL fonts may be bundled in commercial software, apps and games, but not sold on their own; modified fonts remain OFL.
Subsetting a webfont is a modification: permitted, but Reserved Font Names normally cannot be kept; WOFF/WOFF2 wrapping avoids 'modification' only if font data and metadata are unchanged.
When bundling, include copyright statement and licence text (recommended in an About screen with a link).
athar_applications: ATHAR may subset Arabic fonts for the PWA; for fonts with a Reserved Font Name (IBM Plex: 'Plex'; Readex Pro: 'RevReading Lexend') subsets must be renamed — prefer fonts without RFN or serve unmodified files.
limitations: FAQ is guidance, not the licence itself; legal confirmation belongs to library 11.

title: Google Fonts repository — METADATA.pb and OFL.txt for Arabic families (Noto Naskh/Kufi/Sans Arabic, Amiri, Cairo, Tajawal, IBM Plex Sans Arabic, Almarai, Readex Pro)
key_findings: All nine families declare license: OFL with an 'arabic' subset; OFL.txt files confirm SIL OFL 1.1. Copyright lines: Noto (2022 The Noto Project Authors), Amiri (2010-2022 Amiri Project Authors; designers Khaled Hosny, Sebastian Kosch), Cairo (Mohamed Gaber), Tajawal (2018 Boutros International), IBM Plex Sans Arabic (2017 IBM, RFN 'Plex'), Almarai (Boutros), Readex Pro (RFN 'RevReading Lexend').

ATHAR audit with fontTools: Noto Naskh/Kufi/Sans Arabic, Amiri and IBM Plex Sans Arabic cover all 42 base Arabic letters U+0621–U+064A; Cairo, Tajawal, Almarai and Readex Pro lack U+063B–U+063F (rare letters); Tajawal and Readex Pro lack Extended Arabic-Indic (Persian) digits and Tajawal lacks U+066B/U+066C separators.

Arabic+Latin WOFF2 subset sizes: Tajawal 12 KB, Almarai 32 KB, IBM Plex Sans Arabic 41 KB, Noto Naskh 57 KB, Readex Pro 65 KB, Noto Kufi 74 KB, Amiri 90 KB, Cairo 92 KB, Noto Sans Arabic 158 KB (variable fonts carry all weights).
athar_applications: Shortlist for a 3G-friendly PWA: IBM Plex Sans Arabic (UI) or Tajawal (smallest) + Noto Naskh Arabic (long-form documents, diacritics); all OFL, no fee.
limitations: Coverage gaps matter only for rare letters/Persian digits; rendering judged in headless Chromium at 16 px, not with teen readers.

title: Amazon Polly — Available voices (Arabic: Zeina arb standard; Hala and Zayd ar-AE neural)
key_findings: Three Arabic voices: Zeina (arb, female, standard engine) and Hala/Zayd (ar-AE Gulf Arabic, female/male, neural, bilingual).
athar_applications: Option for pre-rendered narration of the tutorial and case 1 (generate offline, ship as audio files).
limitations: Usage/output rights are governed by AWS service terms, not checked here; no Levantine/Egyptian voices listed.

title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech — Supported voices and languages (ar-XA)
key_findings: ar-XA (documented as Modern Standard Arabic) offers about 30 Chirp 3: HD voices plus 4 Standard and 4 WaveNet voices.
athar_applications: Largest MSA voice catalogue found; suitable for MSA narration prototypes.
limitations: Output-rights and pricing not checked; dialect voices not listed under ar-XA.

title: Azure Speech — Language and voice support (Arabic locales)
key_findings: Page (updated 2026-10-22) lists 18 Arabic speech-to-text locales (ar-AE … ar-YE incl. ar-EG, ar-JO, ar-LB, ar-SA, ar-MA); the TTS voice table did not render in our fetch, and the page points to a voices-list API.
athar_applications: Azure's per-country Arabic locales are the broadest regional coverage seen; TTS voice list must be pulled via API before choosing.
limitations: TTS voices not verified in this session (table not retrieved).

title: Open Arabic TTS model licences on Hugging Face: facebook/mms-tts-ara (CC BY-NC 4.0), rhasspy/piper-voices ar_JO 'kareem' (MIT repo; dataset licence unstated), coqui/XTTS-v2 (Coqui Public Model License), fishaudio/fish-speech-1.5 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
key_findings: MMS-TTS Arabic (VITS) is CC BY-NC 4.0 — non-commercial only.

Piper's Arabic voice ar_JO 'kareem' (low/medium) sits in an MIT-tagged repository, but its model card says dataset licence 'See URL' and the linked GitHub repository states no licence — rights unclear.
XTTS-v2 uses the Coqui Public Model License; Fish Speech 1.5 lists Arabic under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
athar_applications: No open, commercially-clear, good-quality Arabic TTS found; if audio is used in v0.1, use a commercial API to pre-render files or record human voice actors (preferred for teen trust).
limitations: Licence tags read from Hub metadata/model cards only; voice quality not tested.
